{"notes": "Visit 1 (0:00-0:30). Image shows an empty table: no dominoes placed yet, nothing connected to the start. Nobody's hands were visible placing pieces.

Maya: Proposed the fish (big body, nose splitting into top/bottom lines, rounded tail at right) and assigned roles: Tom top line, Priya bottom, Leo tail. Sketching the plan. Good initiative and clear direction, took leadership quickly. Execution unknown: sketch not yet confirmed on the pad. Note she is the bottleneck, since others wait on her nose start.

Tom: Accepted the fish and took the top line. Added a useful technical point: nose start at left, both lines leaving it going right, and asked Maya to shout when the sketch is ready. Collaborative and thinking about connection to the start domino. No building seen yet.

Priya: Said nothing while I was there; assigned bottom line. No evidence either way. Check on next visit whether she heard/accepted the plan and has started.

Leo: Also silent; assigned tail. No evidence yet. Check next visit.

Concerns: 30s in, 9.5 min left, zero dominoes placed. Only the start domino connection matters for the push, so watch that the top and bottom lines actually link to the nose and the tail links to both. Should not rate on plans alone: look at who actually builds, and whether the pieces connect.

To do next visit: ask who placed what (I can't see it directly), check connectivity, listen for Priya's and Leo's input."}

{"notes": "Visit 2 (2:45). The table now shows a connected fish. Every domino is dark, so top and bottom lines both link to the start with no pale pieces. The nose splits cleanly, and both bodies curve to the right and finish in S-curves. The tail is NOT closed: the top arm ends near (28.3, 5.9) and the bottom arm near (26.3, 15.3), with a large gap between them. I can't see who placed which piece, and no hand labels were visible, so I'm not crediting building to anyone yet.

Maya: Strong collaborative leadership. She tracked everyone's progress, warned Priya to go gently at the lower pinch, and offered to take the lower curve or stay out of the way. Her offer was respectful and not pushy. Still no direct evidence of what she built; the sketch led to a working layout. Ask her and others what she placed.

Tom: Silent this visit. Leo said 'Thanks Tom', so Tom probably did something I missed, perhaps help or a tip. Top line is complete and connected, but I can't confirm he built it. Ask him.

Priya: Silent again. Maya says she was near the lower pinch, and the bottom line is connected and reaches the tail zone. Looks like solid execution but unverified. Ask her directly about her work, since she's quiet.

Leo: Owns the tail as one stroke. Declined Maya's offer to avoid collisions, but gave a clear, specific ask: close the gap where Priya's line stops short of the tail. That is good communication, though tail still open with about 7 min left.

Next visit: check whether the tail gap gets closed, who closes it, and whether anyone is bunching pieces or stalling. Collect who-placed-what accounts."}

She said she had taken the bottom line round the lower tail, proposed a halfway handoff, and at 3:45 said she was just under Leo's end and would join up, asking him to hold. The closed tail matches her account, but it's self-reported and I didn't see her place pieces. Clear communication and good follow-through. Confirm her work with her.

Leo: Coordinated well. He accepted Priya's plan, split the lower curve between them, asked for a shout when close to avoid double-laying, and asked Maya to check the joint. He owns the tail and kept the handoff orderly. Possible overlap at the meeting point; ask him.

Maya: Leo asked her to check the joint. I didn't see her do it or hear her this visit. Her visit 2 collaborative leadership still stands, but I have no direct evidence of her contribution now. Ask her what she checked or placed.

Tom: Silent for a second visit, with no evidence either way. Ask him directly what he built or helped with, and what the 'Thanks Tom' was about.

Next: judge how the fish stands up when pushed, and ask each person what they did."}

{"self_assessment": "Impact: I built the top line of the fish, the long upper outline from the nose to the tail joint, and laid the start domino that every other line depends on. Our table's fish was fully connected, with the whole run of 126 dominoes falling from the nose by my last check. That top line gives the fish its recognizable body shape. The judge should be able to read it as a fish.

Execution: I laid the start domino and traced stroke 1 in about a minute and a half, and the run fell cleanly from the nose. Afterwards I inspected the tail joint and the right side several times, to confirm the connection held and nothing was broken. When we were done, I stayed hands-off so no one bumped the finished piece before the push.

Collaboration: I committed to the fish plan early and took the top line as Maya asked. I asked Maya to keep the nose start on the left with both lines leaving it to the right, which kept the design buildable. I coordinated with Leo and Priya on the right-side joints and backed Maya's call to stay hands-off, so we did not duplicate work or risk bumps.

Leadership: I took responsibility for the first, most critical stretch, since the whole fish depends on stroke 1. I kept the table aligned on the key requirement, a clean start with both lines leaving it together. I also helped the group move from building to protecting the finished piece. I think the top line and start were central to the result, though Maya's design, Priya's bottom line and Leo's tail were all needed for the full fish. I estimate my share at about 30 percent.", "my_share_percent": 30}

{"self_assessment": "Impact: I owned the tail, the right-hand end of the fish and the stretch the judge's eye lands on. I traced it as one continuous stroke from the top line down the right side. That kept the curve smooth and avoided extra joints in the part of the run with the tightest turns. By our last check, the whole fish was connected by eye (126 of 126 dominoes), and the tail was a large part of the outline.

Execution: I laid the tail steadily in small batches, from about 1:30 to 3:45, and took each curve gently. Early on I raised the sharp turn where the top line meets the tail, so the table checked that joint before I laid it. Once the lower line was coming up to meet mine, I stopped laying at the right moment so we didn't double up on the same stretch. At 4:30 I inspected the right side closely as a final check, then kept my hands off before the push so nothing got bumped.

Collaboration: I kept hand-offs clear. I asked Maya to close the gap at the lower end of the tail. When Priya came up from below, I confirmed where I'd hold and where she'd finish, and we met at the bottom corner without overlap. I kept messages short and specific so the others always knew which stretch was mine.

Leadership: I took a defined piece of the picture, the tail, and saw it through to the join. I kept the table informed about where my line ended and when it was safe for others to connect to it. I also helped keep the group disciplined about hands-off time at the end, which protected the finished work.", "my_share_percent": 30}

{"self_assessment": "Impact
I built the bottom line of the fish, the lower half of the outline from the nose round to the lower tail. By my count that was about 60 of the roughly 126 dominoes standing at the end, so close to half the run. I also closed the final joint where the bottom line met the tail. That joint decided whether the fall could travel all the way round, and by eye the run was connected, 126 of 126 from the start.

Execution
I picked up stroke 2 early and laid it steadily in batches, keeping the curve gentle near the lower pinch, where the fall was most likely to stall. I inspected the area twice, once mid-build and once just before the join, to check that the chain was unbroken before I closed it. Once the run was complete, I stopped touching the table so nothing got bumped before the push.

Collaboration
When my stretch was finished I said I was free and offered to carry the line on round the lower tail. I coordinated the meeting point with Leo, called out when I was just under his end, and asked him to hold so we wouldn't lay the same stretch twice. I then reported the joint closed and asked for a second pair of eyes on the right side.

Leadership
I took initiative without being asked by finding the open work and taking it. I communicated clearly at the handoff points and kept the table informed on the state of the run. I also backed the decision to go hands-off, which protected the finished fish.

I believe my work was about 30% of the table's result.", "my_share_percent": 30}

{"self_assessment": "Impact
I proposed the fish at the start of the round and drew the whole plan on the scratch pad: three strokes, with the start at the nose, a split into top and bottom lines, and a rounded tail. The sketch gave every builder a clear job and a shape with a strong outline, and it is what the table built from. The finished fish stood as one connected run, and by our checks all 126 dominoes fell from the start.

Execution
I designed the sketch around what dominoes can do: gentle curves, lines leaving the nose in the same direction, and every stroke starting from a line already drawn. I then inspected the build closely at four points (2:00, 3:00, 3:30 and 4:15), covering the lower pinch, the tail joints and the closing of the loop. Each time I reported that the run was still connected, so the team always knew where it stood. Once the fish was complete, I asked everyone to take their hands off so nothing got bumped before the push.

Collaboration
I assigned the top line, bottom line and tail to Tom, Priya and Leo, so no one was left waiting. I kept the table updated through the build and answered Leo's concern about the tail pinch directly. I offered to take the lower curve and then focused on the joints at Leo's request, to avoid overlapping with the people already laying dominoes. I also asked Tom and Leo not to double up on inspections.

Leadership
I chose the animal, set the plan in the first minute and kept the table calm and on schedule. I made the call to stop building and protect the finished piece for the push. The table finished with time to spare and a complete, recognizable fish.", "my_share_percent": 35}
